Three, for a final project. Is there a student discount?
There is, if you show me your student card. It takes ten percent off.
Here it is. And do you have many colours in this fabric?
Not many, no. Three, and there is not much of the dark green left.
How much is there? I need three metres and I would rather not change the colour.
Let me measure it. About two and a half. I can order more, but it takes a week.

I have sold fabric to fashion students for about fifteen years, and they all make the same mistake. They buy too little. They calculate exactly what the piece needs, down to the centimetre, and they forget that they are going to cut something wrong at least once. Always buy a bit more than the calculation says. The second thing is money, and this one costs them real money. Most shops around here give students a discount, and almost nobody asks for it. I am not going to offer it if you do not ask, because half the people who come in are not students. Just ask, and show me a card. And the third thing, before you walk out of the door: check the receipt. If the receipt is wrong, or if you lose it, I cannot exchange anything, and every year somebody comes back in tears about a colour they could have changed on the same afternoon.

I had three hundred for the whole final project, and the fabric I fell in love with was two hundred and seventy. So that was that, or so I thought for about a week. What saved it was two decisions. The first one was using a cheaper fabric for the parts nobody sees, the lining and the inside pockets, and keeping the expensive one only for the outside. That alone cut almost a third. The second one was asking for the student discount, which I had never done in my life because it felt like begging. It is not begging. It is a question, and the answer took him four seconds. If I did it again, I would change one thing. I would decide the budget before I fell in love with a fabric, not after. Doing it in that order costs you a week and a lot of arguing with yourself.
